stories: Herman Miller case filed by Attorneys General of New York, Michigan and Illinois in 2008 alleging illegal minimum price-fixing agreements was settled by consent decree only four days after filing, preventing court consideration of Leegin defense
summary: Discussion of antitrust law constraints on pricing practices, including price fixing, vertical price fixing, the Colgate doctrine, and MAP (Minimum Advertised Price) programs. Covers legal precedents and enforcement actions by the FTC and state attorneys general.

actionable_lessons: Companies can treat resellers the same to avoid trade relations risk and legal risk of selective pricing being discovered

Suppliers wishing to provide favorable bid pricing on a selective basis should implement a clearly articulated policy that each piece of bid business is discrete from every other and from everyday sales
A tiered-price program available to competing resellers can be used as a vehicle to permit discrimination in bid pricing
Maintain detailed record-keeping when relying on defenses to price discrimination, as defenses shift the burden of proof to the defendant
Avoid using intermediaries controlled by the ultimate customer to disguise discounts
Avoid situations where an intermediary makes some sales as a wholesaler and others as a retailer while receiving wholesaler discount on all purchases
arguments: MAP programs that are virtually identical and widely used in an industry, suppress almost all forms of price communication, and have demonstrated adverse effects on industry pricing lack procompetitive justification
A tiered-price program available to competing resellers may permit discrimination in bid pricing by favoring those meeting certain criteria
If brand preferences translate into different costs to produce or sell, these costs may be taken into account in pricing through cost justification defense
definitions: Price discrimination: covered by Section 2(a) of the Robinson-Patman Act
Promotional discrimination: addressed under Sections 2(d) and 2(e) of the Robinson-Patman Act
Functional discount: a trade discount based on a purchaser's role in the supplier's distribution system that reflects services performed
Cost justification: a defense that allows pricing differences for otherwise identical products if brand preferences translate into different costs to produce or sell
examples: Pharmaceutical companies paid more than $700 million to settle a consolidated lawsuit brought by drug resellers who alleged that health maintenance and managed care organizations received preferential pricing in violation of the Robinson-Patman Act
Printing, advertising, and real estate are services even though something tangible is involved
Off-the-shelf software is a good, while customized software is most likely a service
A wholesaler may receive a lower price than a direct-buying retailer for functions such as warehousing and taking credit risk
key_points: MAP programs that suppress virtually all forms of price communication and have demonstrated adverse effects on industry pricing lack procompetitive justification
Price discrimination is covered by Section 2(a) of the Robinson-Patman Act, while promotional discrimination is addressed under Sections 2(d) and 2(e)
Direct sales by suppliers to government or charitable organizations for their own use are outside the Robinson-Patman Act
Resellers selling to other businesses in interstate commerce are required to follow the Robinson-Patman Act
The Robinson-Patman Act applies to goods but not services
A defense shifts the burden of proof from plaintiff to defendant
Functional discounts based on distribution system role may be lawful if they reflect reasonable compensation for services provided
names: Volvo Trucks North America, Inc. v. Reeder-Simco GMC, Inc.
Brooke Group v. Brown & Williamson Corp.
Woodman's Food Market, Inc. v. Clorox Co.
open_questions: Whether electricity should be classified as a good or a service in antitrust analysis
What constitutes reasonable compensation for services provided in functional discount arrangements
quotes: they suppress almost all forms of price communication, they have a demonstrated adverse effect on industry pricing, and they lack any procompetitive justification
direct sales by a supplier to the government or a charitable organization (like a not-for-profit school) for its own use are outside the Robinson-Patman Act
a defense shifts the burden of proof from the plaintiff to the defendant

summary: Discussion of MAP (Minimum Advertised Price) programs, Robinson-Patman Act provisions on price discrimination, defenses to price discrimination claims, and distinctions between goods and services in antitrust law.

actionable_lessons: Use quantitative goals in area-of-primary-responsibility contracts rather than vague 'best efforts' language to establish valid vertical restrictions
Ensure pricing communications and data exchanges are transparent and not structured to appear as direct price-fixing discussions
Be aware that loyalty programs can violate antitrust law if used by monopolists to entrench or extend monopoly power
Understand that tying arrangements require five specific elements to be unlawful, including sufficient economic power in the tying product
arguments: Industrial manufacturers consuming supplier products are less likely to be covered under Robinson-Patman promotional discrimination provisions than resellers
Area-of-primary-responsibility contracts with quantitative goals are preferable to vague 'best efforts' clauses for vertical restrictions
The non-public nature and method of operation of data exchange systems can constitute illegal price-fixing if equivalent to direct discussions
definitions: Tying: the sale of one product (the 'tying product') conditioned on the purchase of another (the 'tied product')
Monopolization: requires monopoly power in relevant market and willful acquisition or maintenance of that power
Attempted monopolization: consists of predatory or exclusionary conduct, specific or predatory intent, and dangerous probability of success
Price squeeze: where integrated manufacturer with large market share in key input sells it at higher price to competing manufacturers than it sells its own finished products
examples: Woodman's Food Mkt., Inc. v. Clorox Co. case involving denial of 'club packs' to retailer
Eight airlines and their jointly owned data collection company settled price-fixing case over computerized system for communicating fare changes in advance
key_points: Robinson-Patman Act promotional discrimination provisions apply more commonly to resellers than industrial manufacturers
Suppliers may use written policies to impose vertical restrictions on resellers if they lack written contracts
Monopolists using loyalty programs to entrench or extend monopoly power can violate Section 2 of the Sherman Act
Unlawful tying requires five elements including two separate products and sufficient economic power in the tying product market
Predatory pricing requires proof of pricing below cost and dangerous probability of achieving monopoly power
Price signaling that involves non-public data exchange can be treated as equivalent to direct price-fixing discussions
names: E. I. Du Pont de Nemours & Co.
open_questions: What constitutes sufficient economic power in the tying product market to restrain trade in the tied product market?
How should suppliers balance the use of vertical restrictions with potential trade relations issues?
What level of transparency in pricing communications is required to avoid antitrust liability?
quotes: best efforts clause that requires the reseller to use its best efforts to sell the supplier's products in the reseller's area
the non-public nature of this data exchange and its method of operation were tantamount to the airlines having direct discussions in the same room
